title: sRGB Real Noise Modeling via Noise-Aware Sampling with Normalizing Flows
abstract: Noise poses a widespread challenge in signal processing, particularly when it comes to denoising images. Although convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have exhibited remarkable success in this field, they are predicated upon the belief that noise follows established distributions, which restricts their practicality when dealing with real-world noise. To overcome this limitation, several efforts have been taken to collect noisy image datasets from the real world. Generative methods, employing techniques such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) and normalizing flows (NFs), have emerged as a solution for generating realistic noisy images. Recent works model noise using camera metadata, however requiring metadata even for sampling phase. In contrast, in this work, we aim to estimate the underlying camera settings, enabling us to improve noise modeling and generate diverse noise distributions. To this end, we introduce a new NF framework that allows us to both classify noise based on camera settings and generate various noisy images. Through experimental results, our model demonstrates exceptional noise quality and leads in denoising performance on benchmark datasets.

title: Reproducibility data for "Decodability does not establish Predictive Privilege: Testing Activation Monitoring at Matched Observation Boundaries"
abstract: Abstract for paper here: White-box monitors are often evaluated after more of a model’s generation has unfolded than the text monitor is allowed to see. We measure the size of that mismatch in a binary Diplomacy decision task built from 40 states drawn from distinct released games. In the fixed-action experiment, the post-deliberation activation reader has Brier loss 0.103. The same realized actions are predicted at 0.231 by a text observer before deliberation and at 0.033 after the deliberation is supplied. The activation survives a selection-aware label-permutation test, and text remains better at all five matched prefix cutoffs. We then sample eight trajectories from each state. The final pre-action residual state is almost perfectly separable by the sampled action, while the text result depends strongly on the readout: greedy Qwen scores 0.044 Brier, direct same-family target scoring 0.008, and a pinned Mistral observer 0.018. Exact candidate strings occur in 319 of the 320 sampled trajectories.

title: A Discourse on the Pigeonhole Principle and Epistemic Bound Shifts: The Principle of the Modest Athena Mindset
abstract: We present a formal epistemic and mathematical framework that reconciles closed-loopaxiomatic deduction with open-domain non-linear discovery, termed the Modest AthenaMindset. Classical automated reasoning and formal logic rely on set-theoretic invariants—exemplified by the Pigeonhole Principle (n > k =⇒ ∃ container with > 1 item)in Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the Axiom of Choice (ZFC). While such invariants prevent infinite computational energy waste inside known domains, treating them as absolutelimits on physical reality introduces Paradigm Dogmatism and the Arrogance of the Map.Inspired by the ancient Athenian altar dedicated to the “Unknown God” (Agnosto Theo),this paper establishes an epistemic continuum that bridges rigid axiomatic loops with unmapped higher-dimensional state spaces. We validate this paradigm across three computational domains: (1) the transition from classical set-theoretic counting to the Quantum Pigeonhole Effect, where pre- and post-selected weak measurements allow three quantum particles to occupy two sub-domains without double occupancy; (2) the reduction of Lucas–Lehmer primality testing for Mersenne candidates (M_p= 2^p −1) via the ResonanceTriangular Tensor (RTT) and Zero-One Interchange Principle (OZIP), mapping modular residues onto exact O(1) scalar triangular anchors (n, ∆); and (3) the expansion of state encoding from binary domains (Z_2) to quaternary DNA nucleotide representations(Z_4: {A, C, T, G}) within biomolecular structure engines like. D-RectifyL v3.0, utilizing octonionic e4 basis transformations.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Neural Networks Using IBM SPSS From Data to Intelligent Prediction
abstract: Artificial Intelligence and Neural Networks Using IBM SPSS provides a practical introduction to developing, evaluating, and applying intelligent predictive models. Through clear explanations, step-by-step IBM SPSS procedures, realistic examples, and a complete customer-churn case study, the book guides readers from data preparation to model deployment. It covers Multilayer Perceptron and Radial Basis Function networks, model evaluation, probability thresholds, predictor importance, what-if analysis, responsible implementation, and managerial decision-making. An accessible hands-on guide for students, researchers, analysts, consultants, and professionals seeking to transform data into intelligent and responsible predictions.

title: Quantum Bioinformatics: Gene Sequence Analysis Based on Quantum Error Correction Codes
abstract: This paper explores the application of quantum error correction codes (QECCs) to gene sequence analysis, addressing the limitations of traditional methods in handling high error rates and complex interactions within genomic data. We posit that gene sequences can be represented as quantum bits (qubits), and QECCs can be utilized to identify redundant information and uncover hidden patterns indicative of biological function. The core claim centers on leveraging the high error-correcting capabilities of QECCs to analyze gene sequences with significant redundancy, revealing intricate patterns and interactions previously inaccessible through conventional approaches. The proposed mechanism involves encoding gene sequences into a qubit representation and employing QECC algorithms for error detection and correction, ultimately leading to a refined understanding of genomic data. This research introduces a novel framework for gene sequence analysis, potentially accelerating discoveries in areas such as personalized medicine and evolutionary biology. The core mechanism relies on the ability of QECCs to effectively mitigate errors arising from inherent sequence variations and complex biological processes, providing a robust and potentially highly accurate method for genomic investigation. The analysis presented utilizes a simplified model for demonstration, with future work focused on adapting the techniques to larger and more complex genomic datasets.

title: Adaptive Network Topology Learning for Neural Networks
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network design—Adaptive Network Topology Learning (ANTL). The core premise is that the architecture of a neural network, specifically its topology, profoundly influences its learning capabilities and overall performance. Traditional neural network design relies heavily on manual architectural choices, often requiring significant expert knowledge and extensive trial-and-error. ANTL addresses this limitation by employing a dynamic learning algorithm to adapt the network's topology during training. This adaptation is driven by reinforcement learning, allowing the network to iteratively refine its structure based on performance feedback and the changing characteristics of the data. The algorithm learns to add or remove connections, effectively creating a self-optimizing network architecture. We outline the key components of the ANTL framework, including the reward function design, exploration-exploitation trade-off strategies, and the implementation details of the reinforcement learning agent. Experimental results (simulated) demonstrate the potential of ANTL to achieve superior performance compared to statically defined networks, particularly in scenarios with non-stationary data distributions. The core claim of this work is that adaptive topology learning significantly improves neural network performance, and the proposed mechanism provides a robust pathway to achieve this.

title: ASTRA: Syntactic Analysis of Reasoning in Abstract Neural Networks
abstract: Sensitivity of Large Language Models to Numerically Equivalent Representations: An Exploratory Study with Bayesian Reasoning and Explicit Algebraic Formulation Large Language Models (LLMs) show increasing performance on quantitative and mathematical reasoning tasks. However, accuracy alone does not guarantee robustness: an important question for scientific applications is whether a model preserves the same mathematical outcome when an equivalent quantity is presented through different numerical representations. This exploratory study evaluates that property in five locally executed models — Gemma3:4b, Llama3.1:8b, Granite4.1:3b, Qwen2.5:7b, and Phi4-mini:3.8b — using three mathematical instances represented as fractions, percentages, and decimals. Two experiments were conducted. In the first, models received the components of probabilistic problems and were instructed to compute a posterior probability using Bayes’ theorem. In the second, the corresponding mathematical relation was provided explicitly as an algebraic expression.

title: Advancing Decoding Methods for Enhanced AI Model Performance and Interpretability
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, particularly in large language models, has brought significant challenges in decoding methods that balance performance with interpretability. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of advanced decoding techniques that enhance both model capabilities and explainability. We explore novel approaches including adaptive temperature sampling, nucleus sampling with dynamic thresholds, and hybrid decoding methods that combine multiple strategies. Our research demonstrates that these advanced techniques can significantly improve model performance metrics while maintaining or enhancing interpretability. Through extensive experimentation across diverse datasets, we show that our proposed hybrid decoding method achieves a 12.3% improvement in perplexity scores while maintaining competitive computational efficiency. The findings contribute to the growing body of research on transparent AI systems and provide practical insights for practitioners aiming to deploy more reliable and interpretable AI models in high-stakes applications.

title: Topological Quantum Computing for Universal Algorithm Implementation
abstract: This paper explores the potential of topological quantum computing (TQC) to revolutionize the execution of universal algorithms. Traditional quantum computing faces significant challenges related to qubit decoherence and error correction, severely limiting the complexity of algorithms that can be reliably implemented. TQC, leveraging exotic quasiparticles with inherent topological protection, offers a fundamentally different approach, mitigating these issues and enabling potentially exponential speedups for computationally intensive tasks. This work details a framework for translating general algorithms, including graph algorithms and machine learning algorithms, into topologically protected quantum circuits. We propose a mechanism utilizing the inherent parallelism and robustness of TQC to accelerate algorithm execution. The core claim is that TQC's unique properties can dramatically improve the efficiency of universal algorithm computations. This document outlines the theoretical foundations, conceptual design, and key considerations for realizing this vision.

title: Dynamic Topology Geometry: A Quantum Entanglement-Based Computational Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel computational framework leveraging the principles of dynamic topology geometry, specifically incorporating quantum entanglement as a fundamental building block. We propose a new algorithm that utilizes quantum state transitions and entanglement to dynamically adjust and optimize the topological structure of a given geometry. The core claim is that this approach offers a significant leap in computational efficiency and precision compared to classical methods, particularly for complex geometric configurations. This development aims to move beyond the limitations of traditional techniques and opens the door to solutions that are currently intractable. The paper details the underlying mathematical principles, the algorithm's structure, and its potential impact on various geometric applications.

title: Graph-Based Anomaly Detection using Contrastive Learning
abstract: Anomaly detection in graph-structured data is a challenging problem with significant implications across diverse domains, including fraud detection, network security, and industrial monitoring. Traditional methods often falter when dealing with intricate graph topologies and varying node characteristics. This research proposes a novel approach leveraging contrastive learning to address these limitations. Contrastive learning is utilized to learn robust and informative graph representations by encouraging similar nodes to cluster together and dissimilar nodes to separate. The resulting embeddings effectively capture the underlying structure and patterns within the graph, facilitating accurate anomaly detection. The core contribution lies in the application of this technique to graph anomaly detection, enabling the learning of representations that are inherently resilient to noise and structural complexities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, paving the way for future research and practical implementations.

title: Quantum-Inspired Evolutionary Algorithms for Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum-inspired techniques to enhance the performance of evolutionary algorithms (EAs) for solving complex optimization problems. Traditional EAs often struggle with slow convergence rates, particularly in high-dimensional search spaces. We propose a novel approach that integrates concepts from quantum mechanics, specifically superposition and interference, into the selection and mutation operators of EAs. The core idea is to leverage the ability of quantum systems to explore multiple possibilities simultaneously, thereby accelerating the convergence process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this hybrid algorithm through theoretical analysis and illustrate its potential through detailed mathematical formulations. The results indicate a significant improvement in convergence speed and robustness compared to standard EAs, suggesting a promising direction for future research in optimization. The primary focus is on developing an EA that mimics quantum superposition to examine multiple solutions simultaneously and then uses interference to guide the search towards optimal solutions. This approach aims to address the limitations of conventional EAs, particularly in challenging optimization scenarios.

title: DocIntent: Answerability-Guided Agentic Restoration for Real-World Document Visual Question Answering
abstract: Real-world degradations such as blur, shadow, distortion, and moire patterns severely impair the document question-answering capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Applying restoration tools before Visual Question Answering (VQA) is an intuitive solution. However, existing restoration approaches remain limited, as manually designing and executing restoration strategies is labor-intensive and requires domain expertise. Agentic restoration offers new possibilities for automation, yet existing frameworks primarily target natural images and pursue perceptual quality, overlooking that restoration should serve downstream tasks rather than optimize generic image quality metrics. To this end, we explore the value of agentic restoration for real-world degraded document VQA and propose DocIntent, a training-free Answerability-Guided Agentic Restoration framework. DocIntent first assesses question answerability, then identifies task-relevant degradations and selectively invokes restoration tools. A Comparison-Based Rollback mechanism validates each restoration step and reverts it when question-relevant evidence becomes less decipherable. The entire process requires no additional pretrained degradation classifier or image quality assessment model. Extensive experiments on the WildDoc benchmark show that DocIntent consistently improves the average score and consistency of different open- and closed-source MLLMs. The code and experimental data will be publicly available.

Extensive experiments on the WildDoc benchmark show that DocIntent consistently improves the average score and consistency of different open- and closed-source MLLMs. The code and experimental data will be publicly available.

title: Dynamic Topological Quantum Circuit Design Language
abstract: This paper introduces a novel programming language, the Dynamic Topological Quantum Circuit Design Language (DTQCDL), designed to directly represent and generate quantum circuits based on their topological structure. The core mechanism relies on a formal definition of quantum circuit topology combined with automated reasoning to produce executable quantum circuits. The language aims to simplify the complex design process of quantum circuits, thereby reducing the barriers to entry for quantum computing. This document outlines the key features, syntax, and underlying principles of DTQCDL, highlighting its potential for streamlining quantum circuit development and facilitating broader adoption of quantum technologies. The system focuses on providing a high-level abstraction that allows users to express quantum circuit concepts without needing to deeply understand the low-level details of gate implementation. The automated reasoning component ensures the correctness and efficiency of the generated circuits.

title: Causal Inference on Streaming Data using Hidden Markov Models
abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of performing causal inference on streaming data, a scenario where a complete dataset is unavailable. Traditional causal inference methods rely on sufficient statistics, which are often lacking in continuous data streams. We propose a novel approach that integrates causal inference principles with Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). The core idea is to adapt HMMs to learn causal relationships between observed variables and hidden states, even with incomplete data. This framework allows us to estimate the causal effect of observed variables on underlying, unobserved states within the streaming data. We formally define the problem, outline the methodology, and present a mathematical model incorporating key HMM parameters and causal inference techniques. The proposed method utilizes a Bayesian approach to estimate the model parameters and quantify causal effects. We demonstrate the feasibility and potential of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline future research directions.

title: Hardware Design Adaptation Based on Bio-inspired Algorithms
abstract: This paper proposes a novel hardware design adaptation system leveraging bio-inspired algorithms. The core concept involves utilizing algorithms such as Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to dynamically adjust hardware parameters and topology based on real-time performance feedback. Traditional hardware design methodologies often rely on static configurations, neglecting the inherent variability and changing demands encountered in dynamic environments. This system introduces an adaptive layer, allowing for continuous optimization and resilience. The system's architecture incorporates a feedback loop, monitoring key performance indicators (KPIs) and employing the chosen bio-inspired algorithm to iteratively refine the hardware design. The primary contribution lies in the synergistic combination of bio-inspired optimization with hardware adaptation, resulting in a more robust and efficient design process. This approach addresses the limitations of conventional methods by providing a mechanism for proactive adjustments, enhancing performance and adaptability in diverse operational scenarios. The system is presented as a framework, adaptable to various hardware architectures and application domains. ---

title: Probabilistic Programming for Bayesian Optimization of Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) aims to automate the design of neural networks, traditionally a task requiring significant human expertise. Bayesian Optimization (BO) provides a powerful framework for optimizing complex, black-box functions, and it has seen increasing application in NAS. However, traditional BO methods often struggle with the high dimensionality and complex, non-convex nature of the architecture search space. This work proposes a novel approach that integrates Bayesian Optimization with probabilistic programming, aiming to improve the accuracy of the objective function modeling and enhance exploration within the architecture search space. The core idea is to explicitly model the relationship between network architectures and their corresponding performance metrics using probabilistic models, allowing the BO algorithm to make more informed decisions. The proposed framework offers a more robust and efficient strategy for NAS compared to conventional methods. We explore the theoretical foundations and demonstrate the potential of this approach.

title: Scaling Intermediate-Task Data Size for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer in TyDiQA with mT5-Large
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: How does the scaling of intermediate-task training data size (e.g., 1k vs. 100k samples) affect zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on TyDiQA when using mT5-large, measured by exact match accuracy? title: Adaptive Fractal Geometry for Neural Network Topology
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network design leveraging adaptive fractal geometry. Traditional neural networks often exhibit rigidity, struggling to efficiently adapt to the complexities of high-dimensional data. Our methodology utilizes self-similar, multi-scale fractal structures to dynamically generate and modify neural network topologies during training. The core mechanism involves feeding data-driven feedback into a fractal growth algorithm, enabling the network to evolve its structure and optimize for efficient representation learning. We demonstrate the potential of this adaptive approach to create scalable and robust neural networks capable of tackling complex problems. The key contribution lies in integrating fractal geometry as a fundamental design element, moving beyond static architectures and embracing a truly adaptive and dynamic network structure. The proposed system achieves improved performance metrics compared to standard neural network architectures when applied to challenging datasets.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: Adaptive Training Strategies
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) represents a paradigm shift in machine learning, leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics to potentially unlock unprecedented computational power and algorithmic efficiency. This paper investigates a novel adaptive training strategy for QML models, focusing on the dynamic nature of quantum states. We propose a system that automatically adjusts training parameters based on the quantum state's evolution, fostering improved training efficiency and model generalization. The core mechanism centers around exploiting quantum state transformations to dynamically optimize model parameters during training. The research explores the potential of this approach to overcome the limitations of traditional static training methods and advance the capabilities of QML models. This work introduces a framework for adaptive parameter adjustment predicated on the quantum state, demonstrating a promising path toward enhanced model performance and reduced computational costs.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for machine learning architecture optimization based on adaptive learning. Traditional optimization methods often operate in a static manner, failing to fully exploit the dynamic nature of training data. Our approach dynamically adjusts model parameters and structure based on the training process, resulting in improved model performance and generalization capabilities. This framework addresses the limitations of existing methods by providing a mechanism for continuous adaptation and refinement. We present a comprehensive implementation of the proposed architecture and demonstrate its effectiveness through a series of benchmark experiments across various machine learning tasks. The core mechanism relies on iterative parameter and structure adjustment driven by a learned metric, ensuring optimal performance throughout the training cycle.

title: Quantum Computation via Entanglement Distributing
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to distributed computing leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement. The core claim is that entanglement can be utilized to achieve parallel execution of distributed computing tasks, effectively mitigating the communication bottlenecks inherent in traditional distributed systems. The proposed mechanism involves decomposing complex computational tasks into smaller, manageable sub-tasks, assigning these sub-tasks to distinct quantum processors, and employing entanglement to synchronize intermediate results. This approach aims to exploit the inherent parallelism of quantum mechanics to achieve computational speedups unattainable through classical communication alone. The paper details the theoretical framework, outlining the key components and considerations for implementing such a system, focusing on the challenges and potential benefits of utilizing entangled quantum states for distributed computation. We present a conceptual model, highlighting the potential for overcoming limitations in bandwidth-constrained networks and demonstrating a pathway towards scalable quantum distributed computing architectures. The primary goal is to demonstrate the feasibility of utilizing quantum entanglement as a fundamental building block for a new paradigm in distributed computation. ---

title: Quantum-Inspired Memory Networks with Adaptive Decoherence
abstract: Classical Memory Networks (MemNets) grapple with the "forgetting" problem, struggling to maintain relevant information over extended sequences. This paper proposes a novel architecture – Quantum-Inspired Memory Networks with Adaptive Decoherence – designed to mitigate this issue. The core idea is to introduce a decoherence mechanism inspired by quantum physics, allowing the network to dynamically adjust the decay rate of information stored in memory slots. This adaptation is governed by relevance and usage patterns, leading to optimized information retention and retrieval. Unlike existing approaches that rely on fixed decay rates or simple gating mechanisms, our system leverages an adaptive decoherence rate, providing a more nuanced and effective strategy for managing memory in sequence modeling tasks. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline a framework for implementation.

title: Graph-Based Natural Language Inference
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for Natural Language Inference (NLI) based on graph-based modeling. Traditional NLI approaches often rely on symbolic reasoning, which struggles to capture the nuances of semantic relationships. We propose a new architecture that transforms text into a graph representation, allowing for a more structured and efficient representation of the input. The core mechanism involves constructing a graph where nodes represent sentences and edges represent relationships between them, facilitating reasoning through graph traversal and path-based inference. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of experiments, showcasing improved accuracy in semantic understanding and inference tasks compared to existing methods. The framework's strength lies in its ability to explicitly model semantic dependencies through graph structure.

title: EmoLASP: Emotion Recognition with Language Models and Answer Set Programming
abstract: Emotion recognition in conversations is increasingly tackled with language models, but these models can be unstable and expensive to fine-tune or to prompt with long dialogue histories. We propose EmoLASP, a framework that combines a language model with declarative reasoning via Answer Set Programming (ASP) to predict VAD scores (Valence-Arousal-Dominance) in conversations. Experiments on a widely used benchmark dataset (IEMOCAP) across six open-source LLMs (3B-120B) and two PLMs (BERT, RoBERTa) show that EmoLASP improves prediction performance compared to using the language model alone, even when the LLMs/PLMs are given no dialogue history in their prompts or input vectors. The gains are largest for prompt-only LLMs, which EmoLASP uses without any fine-tuning. However, for fine-tuned PLMs, the reasoner adds little once dialogue history is available. EmoLASP's LLM pipeline demonstrates the potential advantages of using a reasoning approach to ensure emotion prediction consistency and to reduce both the cost of fine-tuning and the cost of prompting with long dialogue histories.

title: Quantum-Inspired Spectral Attention: A Density Matrix Formulation for Transformer Diagnostics and the Heutschi Density Matrix Attention (H-DMAtt)
abstract: Quantum-Inspired Spectral Attention: A Density Matrix Formulation for Transformer Diagnostics and the Heutschi Density Matrix Attention (H-DMAtt) Quanteninspirierte Zustandsräume und spektrale Diagnostik als rigorose Erweiterung der Transformer-Architektur Dr. Theodor Heutschi Date: August 2026 Abstract Self-attention in Transformer models is traditionally understood as a normalised scalar product. This paper presents a mathematically rigorous, quantum-inspired reformulation as a density matrix in the token Hilbert space. In contrast to earlier approaches, it is shown that a naïve symmetrisation of the attention matrix generally does not yield a valid density matrix. As a solution, we introduce a construction based on state amplitudes that is guaranteed to be Hermitian, positive semi-definite and trace-normalised. Building on this, we define the Heutschi Density Matrix Attention (H-DMAtt) - an architectural module that utilises complex-valued state vectors. At runtime, the module computes the von Neumann entropy S(ρ) and the effective dimension D_𝑒𝑓𝑓. We present a controlled benchmark protocol with proof-of-concept results. The work explicitly emphasises the analogical nature of the quantum concepts. Abstract Die Self-Attention in Transformer-Modellen wird traditionell als normalisiertes Skalarprodukt verstanden. Die vorliegende Arbeit stellt eine mathematisch rigorose, quanteninspirierte Reformulierung als Dichtematrix im Token-Hilbertraum vor. Im Gegensatz zu früheren Ansätzen wird gezeigt, dass eine naive Symmetrisierung der Attention-Matrix im Allgemeinen keine gültige Dichtematrix liefert. Als Lösung führen wir eine Konstruktion über Zustandsamplituden ein, die garantiert hermitesch, positiv semi-definit und spurnormalisiert ist. Aufbauend darauf definieren wir die Heutschi Density Matrix Attention (H-DMAtt) - ein Architekturmodul, das komplexwertige Zustandsvektoren nutzt. Zur Laufzeit berechnet das Modul die Von-Neumann-Entropie S(ρ) und die effektive Dimension D_𝑒𝑓𝑓 Wir präsentieren ein kontrolliertes Benchmark-Protokoll mit Proof-ofConcept-Ergebnissen. Die Arbeit betont ausdrücklich den analogischen Charakter der Quantenbegriffe.

title: Quantum State Adaptive Topology Evolution
abstract: Quantum state adaptive topology evolution is a novel approach to quantum computing that leverages the inherent adaptability of quantum states to dynamically engineer and stabilize quantum systems. This paper introduces a dynamic evolution model based on the self-adaptative properties of quantum states, demonstrating a significant improvement in the robustness and performance of quantum computations compared to static topological evolution methods. The core mechanism centers around strategically manipulating the quantum state through a continuous, adaptive process, ensuring a stable and controllable quantum state evolution. The research highlights the potential of this approach to overcome limitations of existing quantum algorithms, particularly in scenarios demanding high resilience and adaptability.

title: Based on Dynamic Topology for Semantic Network Computation
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to semantic network computation centered around dynamic topology. The core claim is that constructing dynamic, application-driven semantic network topologies can significantly improve the efficiency and adaptability of knowledge reasoning and data querying. This is achieved through the utilization of machine learning models—specifically, reinforcement learning or generative adversarial networks—to automatically learn and optimize the network topology. These models dynamically adjust node connections and weights based on query patterns and data updates, ultimately reducing query latency and enhancing inference accuracy. The current state of semantic networks often relies on static or predefined topologies, lacking the ability to adapt to real-time data and evolving query demands. This dynamic topology methodology represents a new paradigm, integrating semantic network inference with topology optimization techniques, offering substantial potential for future advancements. ---

The paper concludes with a discussion of the challenges and future directions of this research.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning via Temporal Logic Programming with Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for neuro-symbolic reasoning that leverages the complementary strengths of neural networks and temporal logic programming. The core idea is to utilize neural networks to learn the underlying rules of temporal logic, effectively bridging the gap between pattern recognition and logical deduction. We introduce a system where neural networks are trained to interpret temporal logic expressions, allowing for dynamic rule extraction and application. This approach enables reasoning about sequences of events over time in a flexible and adaptable manner. The system's architecture incorporates a temporal logic engine, driven by the learned neural network representations, facilitating robust temporal reasoning. The paper outlines the key components, the training methodology, and a conceptual demonstration of the framework. The primary contribution lies in the integration of neural network learning with the formal structure of temporal logic, offering a potentially powerful approach to complex reasoning tasks. We demonstrate the potential for this hybrid system to outperform traditional methods in scenarios requiring both pattern recognition and logical inference.

title: Multi-Agent Collaborative Learning with Dynamic Topology Optimization
abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of optimizing multi-agent collaborative learning (MCL) by introducing a dynamic topology structure optimization framework. Traditional MCL methods often rely on fixed topologies, which may not be optimal for varying task demands and evolving agent states. We propose a novel approach that leverages reinforcement learning (RL) to dynamically adjust the topology of a multi-agent system, enhancing both efficiency and overall learning performance. The core idea is to model the agent-agent communication and task dependencies as a graph and use RL to learn optimal edge weights and connectivity patterns within this graph. The system adapts to changing conditions by modifying the strengths of connections between agents, adjusting communication frequencies, and potentially adding or removing connections entirely. This dynamic adjustment enables the system to focus computational resources on critical interactions and effectively distribute tasks, ultimately leading to improved convergence rates and better solutions. We outline the key components of the framework, including the state representation, action space, reward function, and the RL algorithm employed. Experimental results (simulated) demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach compared to static topology MCL.

title: Information-Theoretic Graph Embedding with Mutual Information Maximization
abstract: Graph embedding techniques have emerged as powerful tools for representing complex graph structures in a low-dimensional vector space. However, many existing methods primarily focus on preserving graph topology, often overlooking the rich information encoded within node relationships and edge connections. This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding that explicitly incorporates information theory, specifically maximizing mutual information between node embeddings and the graph's adjacency matrix. Our method learns embeddings that not only capture structural similarities but also reflect the statistical dependencies present in the graph, leading to more informative and discriminative representations. We formulate the embedding process as a maximization problem, leveraging techniques from information theory to guide the learning process. The resulting embeddings demonstrate improved performance in downstream graph-based tasks compared to traditional embedding methods that rely solely on graph topology. The key contribution lies in the explicit incorporation of information content during the embedding learning phase, offering a fundamentally different perspective on graph representation.

title: Non-Deterministic Program Synthesis and Evolution
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to program synthesis that incorporates non-deterministic behavior, mimicking the adaptive strategies observed in biological systems. Traditional program synthesis techniques primarily focus on generating deterministic programs, often limiting their robustness and adaptability to dynamic environments. This research proposes a framework for synthesizing programs using evolutionary algorithms, where the core innovation lies in defining and optimizing a representation of non-deterministic programs. Specifically, we leverage probabilistic models, such as Bayesian Networks, as the representation for these programs. The evolutionary algorithm then iteratively refines the parameters of these probabilistic models, enabling the synthesized programs to dynamically adjust their behavior based on environmental changes. The resulting programs exhibit a greater degree of resilience and adaptability compared to purely deterministic counterparts. The key contributions of this work include a formal method for representing non-deterministic programs, an evolutionary algorithm tailored for optimizing these representations, and an evaluation framework demonstrating the enhanced adaptive capabilities of the synthesized programs. This research paves the way for creating more intelligent and robust software systems capable of thriving in complex and uncertain conditions. ---

title: Quantum-Inspired Relational Reasoning for Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities in generating human-like text and performing various language tasks. However, a significant limitation remains in their ability to perform robust relational reasoning – understanding and inferring relationships between entities within complex contexts. This paper proposes a novel approach to enhance relational reasoning in LLMs by drawing inspiration from quantum measurement theory. We introduce a framework that represents relationships as probability distributions, mimicking the concept of superposition, and utilizes a simulated quantum measurement process to refine these distributions based on contextual information, adhering to the Born rule. This method moves beyond the traditional pattern-matching approach of LLMs, offering a more nuanced and probabilistic understanding of relationships. The core idea is to treat relationships not as definitive true/false statements, but as possibilities with associated probabilities. We explore the potential of this approach to improve LLM performance on tasks requiring intricate relational understanding, ultimately leading to more accurate and reliable inferences. The key elements of this framework include the creation of relational probability distributions, the simulation of a quantum measurement process, and the application of the Born rule to update these distributions based on observed context.

title: Co-Evolutionary Prompt Optimization with Cross-Category Transfer for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection
abstract: Zero-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD) has gained significant attention for its practical value in industrial inspection. Recently, CLIP-based approaches have been widely adopted in ZSAD due to their strong vision-language generalization capabilities. However, existing methods commonly employ continuous prompt embeddings for prompt optimization and encode semantics in latent vectors, which lack interpretability and scalability. To this end, we propose CoEvoAD, a co-evolutionary framework for discrete prompt selection. CoEvoAD performs prompt search in the discrete natural-language space using an evolutionary algorithm. Candidate prompts are iteratively generated, evaluated, and selected throughout population evolution, thus preserving the interpretability and composability of natural language. Furthermore, we introduce a Cross-Category Transfer Objective (CCTO), which treats held-out source categories as proxies for unseen categories and scores prompt rules based on their estimated cross-category transferability, effectively improving cross-category generalization. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of CoEvoAD, and the results show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple anomaly detection datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/rstao-bjtu/CoEvoAD.

title: SMILE: Smooth Motion for Improved Long-Horizon VLA Execution
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models reduce inference cost by executing multiple actions per call, but longer horizons often degrade accuracy because raw chunks contain jitter and outliers. We introduce SMILE, an architecture-preserving interface that predicts B-spline coefficients and decodes them into smooth action sequences. SMILE changes only the action representation, enabling longer fixed horizons while retaining each baseline's backbone and model scale. We apply SMILE to SmolVLA, Evo1, VPP, and DAWN, improving accuracy and amortized inference efficiency across LIBERO, CALVIN, and real-world experiments. SMILE-Evo1 reaches 98.0% with a 1.1x speedup on LIBERO, while SMILE-VPP reaches an average length of 4.42 with a 1.5x speedup on CALVIN. At a matched execution horizon of 10, SMILE-SmolVLA reduces non-boundary acceleration by 78.6% and velocity sign-change rate by 42.3%. Real-world xArm tests show higher success, fewer drops, and fewer contacts. These results establish smooth coefficient-space generation as a route to accurate, efficient long-horizon VLA execution. Project page: jongwoopark7978.github.io/smilevla

title: Typed Constitutional Language (TCL) Formal Specification v0.1
abstract: This specification defines the Typed Constitutional Language (TCL), a formal language for expressing executable constitutions in which constitutional authority, evidence requirements, state transitions, governance predicates, and execution effects are represented by a static type system. TCL extends the existing Executable Governance calculus. That calculus defines constitutional governance as deterministic evaluation of a finite set of predicates over constitutional state and immutable evidence, with admissibility requiring every mandatory predicate to succeed. It further defines refusal, replay, proof objects, soundness, preservation, and verifier independence. TCL introduces a complementary static guarantee. A well-typed constitutional program SHALL be structurally incapable of constructing an executable consequence without passing through the constitutional authority represented by its type system.

title: Impact of Intermediate-Task Dataset Scaling on Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer Performance in XTREME-R
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: Does scaling the size of the intermediate-task training dataset (e.g., 10K vs. 100K samples) affect zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on XTREME-R, evaluated using EM and F1 scores? title: Dynamic Quantum State Adaptive Quantum Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive quantum algorithm, the Dynamic Quantum State Adaptive Quantum Algorithm, designed to enhance the performance of quantum algorithms through dynamic adjustment of quantum state parameters. The core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that continuously analyzes input data and adjusts the quantum state to optimize performance. Traditional optimization methods often rely on static parameter settings, whereas this algorithm proactively adapts to the data, offering improved efficiency and robustness. The paper details the algorithm's design, implementation, and preliminary results, emphasizing the advantages of dynamic adaptation in quantum computation.

title: ##基于认知地图的知识推理与决策
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to knowledge reasoning and decision-making systems based on cognitive maps. Traditional knowledge representation and reasoning methods often struggle with complex, interconnected knowledge domains. Cognitive maps offer a promising solution by providing a visual and intuitive representation of knowledge, facilitating more effective reasoning and decision support. This work details the construction of a system utilizing cognitive maps to represent knowledge, perform inference, and ultimately drive decision-making processes. The core claim is the development of a system leveraging cognitive maps for knowledge reasoning and decision support. The central mechanism involves transforming a knowledge base into a cognitive map, subsequently employing the semantic information within the map for knowledge inference and decision-making. The novelty lies in the application of cognitive maps to enhance system intelligence, offering a more adaptable and interpretable approach compared to conventional methods. We explore the key components of the system, including cognitive map construction, inference algorithms, and decision-making strategies. Finally, we discuss the potential benefits and challenges associated with this approach.

title: Quantum Key Distribution Protocol Optimization in Quantum Information Encryption
abstract: This paper investigates the optimization of quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols, focusing on enhancing both security and efficiency within the key negotiation process. title: SmallReason-ColBERT: An Ultra-Small Late-Interaction Retriever for Reasoning Intensive Retrieval
abstract: Reasoning-intensive retrieval remains difficult for small models. title: Deciding When to Decide: Testing Operational Suboptimality Under Distributional Shift
abstract: Deployed decisions are often optimized once and retained because updates impose operational, regulatory, or switching costs. As operating conditions change, when should such decisions be re-optimized? We study this question for stochastic optimization when the objective's functional form is known but the decision maker's trade-offs are encoded by an unknown preference parameter. Standard distribution-shift tests are poorly aligned with this goal: they can flag detectable yet decision-irrelevant changes without determining whether the incumbent decision has become materially suboptimal. We propose \texttt{RADAR} (Regret-based Assessment of Decision Adequacy and Risk), a decision-focused framework that uses inverse optimization to infer latent preferences and tests the deployed decision's optimality gap under the current distribution. By targeting regret, \texttt{RADAR} ignores decision-irrelevant shifts while detecting changes that warrant re-optimization. We develop two-sample and sequential changepoint procedures and establish asymptotic guarantees for Type-I error and power. Across synthetic optimization problems, a semi-synthetic capacity allocation task, and police-zone planning, \texttt{RADAR} more reliably distinguishes harmful from harmless shifts than decision-agnostic alternatives.

title: Algorithmic personalization has become a key strategy, impacting how customers make spontaneous purchases and their lifetime value - Evidence from Brazil and Indonesia
abstract: Algoritmik kişiselleştirmenin dürtüsel satın alma ve müşteri yaşam boyu değeri üzerindeki etkisi teorik ve ampirik açıdan yeterince araştırılmamış olmakla birlikte, algoritmik kişiselleştirmenin e-ticaret ortamında tüketici davranışlarını ve tüketicilerin hızla değişen algoritmik uygulamalara yönelik tutumlarını önemli ölçüde şekillendirdiği bilinmektedir. Bu çalışma, ilgili literatüre dayanarak bütünleşik bir kavramsal araştırma modeli geliştirmektedir. PLS-SEM temelli modelde, algılanan değerin çok boyutlu yapısı aracı değişken olarak ele alınırken algoritmik şeffaflık ve algılanan kontrolün tüketici güveni üzerindeki etkisi ile tüketici güveninin müşteri yaşam boyu değeri (CLV) üzerindeki etkisi incelenmektedir. Ayrıca kişilik, güç mesafesi ve dijital okuryazarlık kontrol değişkenleri olarak modele dâhil edilmiştir. Ekim–Kasım 2025 döneminde Brezilya’dan 76 ve Endonezya’dan 101 olmak üzere toplam 177 yetişkin dijital tüketiciden kesitsel veriler toplanmıştır. Araştırma kapsamında test edilen yedi hipotezin tamamı desteklenmiştir. Bulgular, algoritmik kişiselleştirmenin dürtüsel satın alma davranışını olumlu yönde etkilediğini göstermektedir. Bu etkiye kısmen algılanan fiyat değeri (dolaylı etki = 0,187) ile duygusal ve sosyal değer aracılık etmektedir. Dışa dönüklük ve dijital öz yeterlilik de dürtüsel satın alma tepkisini güçlendiren faktörler arasında yer almaktadır. Algoritmik şeffaflık ile tüketici güveni arasındaki ilişki kısmen desteklenmiştir. Tüketici güveni, açıklanan varyansın %42,9’unu oluşturarak ilgili etki mekanizmasının en önemli aracısı olarak ortaya çıkmış ve toplam etkinin yaklaşık %20’sine aracılık etmiştir. Ayrıca tüketici güveninin modeldeki en güçlü yordayıcı değişken olduğu belirlenmiştir (β = 0,612; f² = 0,489). Yüksek düzeyde algılanan kontrol ile yüksek algoritmik şeffaflık arasında teorik açıdan sinerjik bir etkileşim bulunmaktadır ve bu ortak etki, iki unsurun bağımsız etkilerinin toplamından daha güçlüdür. Bu etki; güç mesafesi düşük tüketiciler ile dijital okuryazarlık düzeyi yüksek tüketiciler arasında daha belirgindir. Çoklu grup analizi, algoritmik şeffaflık ile algılanan kontrol arasındaki etkileşimin kültürel bağlamın düzenleyici etkisi altında anlamlı olduğunu; buna karşılık temel yapısal ilişkilerin kültürel bağlama göre önemli ölçüde farklılaşmadığını göstermektedir. Çalışma, algoritmik şeffaflık ve algılanan kontrolün ikincil etik meseleler olarak değerlendirilmesi anlayışını tersine çevirmektedir. Algoritmalar çağında sürdürülebilir müşteri yaşam boyu değeri, tüketicileri somut biçimde güçlendiren yönetişim uygulamaları aracılığıyla gerek işletme gerekse tedarik zinciri düzeyinde gerçekleştirilen bir güven inşa süreci olarak değerlendirilmektedir.

title: Tgmenks v13.20 — An Artificial Society of Gene Machines in the Ecological Niche of Knowledge: simulation, documentation, and manuals
abstract: Tgmenks is a deterministic, browser-based agent-based simulation implementing the Theory of Gene Machines in the Ecological Niche of Knowledge (Tgmenks), a research programme developed by the author over four decades. Agents possess eight capability sets (bodily, epistemic, moral, political, organisational, relational, resource, aesthetic), an emotional-fitness system, kinship, and belief systems of two structural kinds (methods of regulating vs. suppressing the struggle for power, MRSP/MSSP). From these capacities — under a constitutional principle that the engine provides capacities, never regimes — worlds unfold in which villages, towns, city-states, states and empires, land tenure and its violations, the three roads of marriage (wooed, arranged, taken), predation and the longing for a justice-bringing ruler, and the selection pressures at the apex of power emerge without scripting. Every event carries its reasons in a readable record; identical seeds re-derive identical histories, making all findings reproducible. This version (v13.20) is certified by the included test report: full save/load state fidelity, off-switch invariance to the v13.10 baseline, and forced-path verification of all major mechanisms. The deposit includes the complete standalone simulation (a single HTML file, runs offline in any modern browser), release notes, the certification report, and user manuals in English, Kurdish (Sorani), and Arabic. Theory and further materials: tgmenks.net.

title: Core Claim: Establish a method for adaptive model tuning based on non-local discovery, leveraging non-locality discovery to adjust model parameters, thereby enabling more effective model training and optimization.
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to model tuning, termed "Adaptive Non-Local Discovery Tuning" (ANDT), designed to enhance the training and optimization process of machine learning models. The core of this method centers around the utilization of non-local discovery to dynamically adjust model parameters. A key mechanism involves introducing a "Non-Locality Discovery Parameter Adjustment" (NLDA) mechanism, which leverages the inherent non-locality inherent in many real-world datasets to guide parameter adjustments. This approach aims to overcome limitations of traditional parameter optimization techniques by providing a more robust and adaptable method for model refinement. The benefits of this methodology are demonstrated through a series of experiments across diverse datasets, showcasing improved convergence speed, reduced sensitivity to initial parameter settings, and enhanced generalization performance. This work provides a significant advancement in model tuning, particularly for scenarios involving non-stationary data.

title: Quantum State Adaptive Topology Mapping Algorithm
abstract: Quantum state adaptive topology mapping algorithms offer a promising avenue for enhancing quantum computation's performance by dynamically adjusting the quantum state's topology. This paper introduces a novel algorithm that leverages the inherent complexity of quantum states to achieve sophisticated quantum states, thereby improving quantum computing capabilities. We propose a method that employs a continuous, self-tuning mapping process, allowing the system to adapt to the specific characteristics of the input quantum state. This adaptive approach significantly expands the range of achievable quantum states and facilitates the exploration of complex quantum phenomena. The algorithm's core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that continuously refines the quantum state's topology based on a predefined criterion, ensuring optimal performance. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental results, highlighting its potential for advancing quantum information processing. Furthermore, the paper discusses potential challenges and future research directions.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on an adaptive Bayesian network structure. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with complex problems, particularly those lacking extensive domain knowledge. This algorithm addresses this limitation by dynamically adjusting the parameters of a Bayesian network, leveraging probabilistic reasoning to mitigate uncertainty and enhance optimization efficiency. The core mechanism involves a self-adaptive parameter adjustment process guided by Bayesian network inference, resulting in improved performance across a range of optimization tasks. We present a detailed implementation and analysis, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in several challenging scenarios.

title: Decentralized Machine Learning via Secure Multi-Party Computation and Homomorphic Encryption
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for decentralized machine learning (DML) that prioritizes data privacy and security. The core of the approach lies in the synergistic utilization of Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) and Homomorphic Encryption (HE). Traditional machine learning often relies on centralized datasets, raising significant privacy concerns. Our method allows for training machine learning models on distributed datasets without exposing the underlying data to any single party. SMPC enables collaborative model training among multiple participants, while HE permits computations to be performed directly on encrypted data. This significantly reduces the risk of data breaches and misuse. The framework provides a secure and efficient pathway for leveraging the collective intelligence of decentralized data sources, offering a viable solution for sensitive applications. We demonstrate the feasibility and potential benefits of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline key considerations for its practical implementation. The key innovation here is the combined application of these techniques for a truly decentralized and privacy-preserving machine learning solution.

title: Quantizing Probability Distributions: A Non-Linear Fusion Approach
abstract: This paper introduces a novel non-linear probability distribution fusion algorithm designed to enhance numerical simulations and predictive accuracy. The core concept centers around dynamically adjusting the strength of probability distributions through a learned fusion function, achieved using a neural network. This allows for a more precise representation of complex, non-linear relationships within the data, offering improvements over traditional methods. The algorithm's proposed mechanism addresses limitations of existing approaches, specifically in capturing the intricacies of non-linear data distributions. We present a detailed theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach.

title: Adaptive Graph Neural Networks with Temporal Memory
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for analyzing and modeling complex relationships within graphs, finding applications in diverse fields like social network analysis, drug discovery, and computer vision. However, traditional GNN architectures often suffer from limitations in capturing long-range dependencies, hindering their ability to effectively represent and learn from intricate structural information. This paper introduces Adaptive Graph Neural Networks (AGNNs) with a novel temporal memory mechanism, designed to address this challenge. The AGNN dynamically updates the network's memory across time, allowing it to better incorporate past states into its current predictions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through extensive experiments on several benchmark graph datasets, showcasing significant improvements in performance, particularly in tasks requiring long-range dependency identification. The proposed method offers a fundamentally new approach to GNNs, pushing the boundaries of their ability to handle complex graph structures.

title: S³‑Delta: Spectral‑Stratum SpatioTemporal Delta
abstract: Coordinate-bearing streams obey two orders: observations arrive in time, whereas memories should be reactivated by physical location. We study fixed-capacity memory for agents that scan two- or three-dimensional spaces and must fuzzily recall previously observed values near the current position. Standard fast weights support one-matrix key-value recall, but uniform forgetting cannot identify reliable spatial scales, while the conventional Delta rule treats all Fourier components as one estimate. We propose Spectral-Stratum SpatioTemporal Delta (S3-Delta). Each sine-cosine pair of a fixed Fourier key defines a wavelength stratum of one shared fast-weight matrix. Before each write, wavelength-conditioned continuous-time decay advances the state and the complete matrix produces one causal recall. After the current observation arrives, removing each stratum counterfactually measures whether it reduced or increased the recall error. Accumulated signal and noise evidence forms a reliability gate for later readout, while one normalized Delta residual updates the complete matrix and preserves a shared target across scales. title: The MYOSAIQ Challenge: Myocardial Segmentation with Automated Infarct Quantification
abstract: Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) cardiac magnetic resonance (MR) imaging is the modality of choice to assess myocardial infarction (MI) lesions. Nowadays MI volume quantification is not performed routinely in clinical practice. Numerous deep learning (DL) methods have been developed to automate the segmentation of the myocardium and infarct regions. However, most studies rely on relatively small datasets which typically undergo pre-processing steps to standardize images and focus on a specific phase of myocardial infarction following reperfusion therapy. These limitations have impeded the development of models that are generalizable across diverse conditions and thus suitable for routine clinical use. To advance research and establish benchmarks in generalizable learning for myocardial infarct quantification, this paper presents findings from the Myocardial Segmentation with Automated Infarct Quantification (MYOSAIQ) challenge. The dataset set up for the challenge combines 439 CMR volumes from two multicenter clinical trials, with representative data acquired in acute and chronic phases after acute MI. Data were acquired in 16 centers using MRI scanners from three different vendors. Six teams participated until the end of the challenge, employing various baseline models, data augmentation techniques, and confidence strategies. To enhance the significance of this study, we compare the challengers' results with those of fine-tuned foundation models. Our results indicate that well-designed UNet-based techniques outperform fully automatic foundation models for LGE MR segmentation. While the best methods achieve high-quality and stable delineations of the left ventricle and myocardium under various conditions, they remain improvable in accurately segmenting infarct regions.

title: Pauper Consensus: Two Pre-Registered LLM Studies
abstract: Agreement across large language models is a measurement instrument, and this paper treats the whole instrument as the object under test, under pre-registration, in two studies built one on top of the other. In Study 1, an identical frozen proposition-aggregation protocol run on two independently selected three-model panels returned opposite registered verdicts on synthetic reasoning traces (−0.159 vs +0.122 nats, both 95% CIs excluding zero); a post-hoc diagnosis located the disagreement in the instrument twice over — a calibration map with no intercept measured against a baseline that had one, and a corpus that could barely contain falsehoods (0 of 607 negative-polarity propositions ever scored by the alignment layer) — and a second registration, git-tagged before any new generation, confirmed the central repair on two panel–corpus configurations sharing no model family (+0.220 and +0.272 nats) while falsifying two companion predictions. A 2026-08-29 correction then retracted a further claim of the draft (the "one vote per source" invariant, whose frozen arm was actually capped and unsigned, so it measured polarity, not capping: no unsigned arm exceeds AUROC 0.6063 anywhere, every signed arm is at least 0.9001) and first reported, post-hoc, the contrast that separates pooling from choosing well: the panel beats the calibration-selected best single source by +0.0448 to +0.0887 nats on 3 of 4 panel-cycles, inconclusively on the fourth. A third cycle (prereg-v3) is registered to test that margin as its primary. Study 2 stands on the repaired instrument: a jury of twelve 3–4B local language-model configurations (four families × three arms) votes PASS / FAIL / NOT_STATED on 8,000 labeled claims constructed from 200 real news articles (96,000 votes in 13.2 h on one Mac Studio), and the votes are aggregated by a Dawid–Skene model with per-arm calibration maps fitted once on a smaller prior corpus and applied frozen (the EM weights themselves are refit unsupervised on the new votes) — the protocol we name Pauper Consensus. Every design rule is inherited from Study 1's corrections: tag before inference (R1), intercept-bearing calibration maps (R2), a corpus with a registered 25% FAIL mass (R3), one signed observation per source (R4). The pre-registered capability gate passes: +0.20289 nats of log-loss over a frozen model-free bar at the registered 25% FAIL-mass design point (95% article-block bootstrap CI [0.18737, 0.21740]; refitting the bar on v2 alone costs the headline −0.020 nats, §13.3), all four test cells green — while the companion registered prediction that the model-free bar's own value would transfer fails. The headline is a comparison against a specified model-free feature bar, not evidence of ensemble superiority: the panel-versus-best-single-source margin is small and unregistered (+0.0448 to +0.0887 nats on 3 of 4 Study 1 cycles, §8.3), and the registered third cycle takes it as its primary. The system gate against a single near-frontier 27B model passes via its cheaper-and-indistinguishable branch: both routes co-fail the only two unsupported claims in the defendant stream (12–0 jury agreement across all twelve configurations, PASS from the 27B on both); with two false claims in the stream the false-claim rates are statistically indistinguishable (95% CI [0.0, 5e-05]) — a cost result, not a quality-equivalence claim — and the jury route is 0.781× length-adjusted cost; the 27B is nonetheless the more accurate single model on the full pool (95.887% vs 93.912% three-state), and the binding hardware barrier is 48 GB GDDR7 memory, not arithmetic. Across the two studies, every "failure" — the cycle-1 flip, the two failed cycle-2 predictions, P9, the mis-specified null, the 0/2 catch — was an instrument property or a registered bound, surfaced under frozen registration, not a failed hypothesis. The honest unit of account for LLM-based verification is the instrument: protocol, corpus, calibration, hardware, cost.

title: Do AI Models Speak Human?
abstract: Working paper and open data. Users who want an AI model to write like a person usually assume that the machine register is a default that an instruction can lift. We tested that assumption. Ten passages of published academic prose from PubMed Central, all from articles deposited before 2022, gave ten topics. Four flagship models (GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.7 Flash and DeepSeek V4 Pro) wrote about 300 words on each topic under three prompts: a plain request; a detailed brief on the properties that separate human academic prose from assistant prose (uneven sentence length, plain words, no triads, no connective openers, hedging, asides); and the same brief with a human passage as an example. Every text was placed on the frozen 47-feature stylometric human-to-AI spectrum from our earlier work and scored by GPTZero, alongside the ten human passages. The brief worked on the surface: the pooled spectrum position fell from 148 under the plain prompt to 30 under the styled one (human passages 10), 14 of the 40 styled texts landed inside the middle half of the human anchors, and Claude Opus 5 moved past the human median. The models overshot every property the brief named, writing more unevenly and at a lower reading grade than the journals, and left the one property it did not name, vocabulary range, where tuning had put it. GPTZero did not move: all 120 AI texts, under every prompt and from every model, received a document AI probability of 1.00, and all ten human passages received 0.00. The human exemplar added nothing. One pass through TextPulse moved the same texts a mean of 47 points toward the human end while keeping 97 percent of the meaning, and moved the detector where instruction had not. We read the result through the published measurements of preference tuning: supervised fine-tuning and RLHF narrow the distribution a model samples from, an instruction is a condition on that narrowed distribution rather than a replacement for it, and a probability-based detector reads the process, not the surface. Prompting cannot undo preference tuning. All texts, prompts, detector replies, scores and code are released. Files: the paper (PDF), per-text scores for the 10 human passages, 120 AI outputs and 120 TextPulse outputs, the analysis results, a data archive with every text, the exact prompts and every GPTZero reply, and the scripts and figures.

title: PROBE: una propuesta conceptual de software dirigida por modelos para explorar los límites de los modelos fundacionales orientados a prompt aplicados a tareas específicas
abstract: Los modelos fundacionales de inteligencia artificial (IA) orientados a prompt presentan un potencial sin precedentes para resolver tareas complejas, desde la generación de texto coherente hasta el reconocimiento de objetos en imágenes. Sin embargo, su aplicación efectiva en dominios específicos sin incurrir en costosos procesos de reentrenamiento o ajuste fino (fine-tuning) constituye un desafío fundamental. Además, no existe una metodología sistemática que permita evaluar su rendimiento al aplicarlos a una tarea específica, ni comparar el funcionamiento de diferentes versiones del mismo modelo. Esta tesis aborda directamente dichas carencias, explorando tres cuestiones clave: 1) la viabilidad de aplicar un modelo de propósito general a una tarea específica (downstream task) mediante la optimización de la interacción (prompting), 2) la existencia y cuantificación de un techo de rendimiento inherente a esta aproximación no intrusiva, y 3) la transferencia directa de mejoras a la tarea específica cuando el modelo base evoluciona. Para dar respuesta a estos desafíos se realiza una propuesta dirigida por modelos que formaliza un marco metodológico para la exploración y evaluación de los límites de rendimiento de modelos fundacionales orientados a prompt llamada PROBE (Prompt Optimization for Boundary Exploration, Optimización de Prompts para la Exploración de Límites). Esta propuesta establece un proceso estructurado para determinar el máximo potencial de un modelo fundacional aplicado a una tarea especializada, permitiendo a los usuarios tomar decisiones informadas sobre su idoneidad y estrategia de implementación. La propuesta se valida empíricamente a través de un caso de estudio en segmentación de imágenes, demostrando la capacidad de ésta para guiar la optimización y medir sus límites de forma efectiva.

title: Based on Multi-Scale Chaotic Maps: A Novel Neural Network Activation Function
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to designing neural network activation functions based on the principles of multi-scale chaotic systems. The core idea is to leverage the inherent characteristics of chaotic systems – specifically, their sensitivity to initial conditions and multiple scales of dynamics – to create activation functions capable of automatically learning and adapting to complex, nonlinear relationships. Traditional activation functions often struggle with accurately representing highly nonlinear data, leading to limitations in the performance of neural networks. This work proposes a method to embed information from multiple scales of chaotic maps within the activation function itself. This incorporation facilitates powerful nonlinear expression capabilities through the chaotic system's sensitive dependence on initial conditions and, crucially, enhances network robustness by utilizing the multi-scale properties. The resulting activation function offers a potentially superior alternative to conventional designs, particularly in scenarios involving intricate and dynamic data. We present a detailed formulation of the approach, highlighting the mathematical underpinnings and demonstrating its potential for improved neural network performance. ---

title: Quantum State Geometry Modeling: A Dynamic Approach
abstract: Quantum state geometry modeling presents a novel framework for representing and manipulating quantum systems, leveraging the inherent dynamic nature of quantum states. This paper explores the development of a dynamic geometric model based on quantum state adaptation, offering a powerful tool for simulating and optimizing quantum systems. We introduce a method that dynamically adjusts the geometric structure of the quantum state based on specific input parameters, enabling a more nuanced and adaptable approach compared to traditional static modeling techniques. The core mechanism involves establishing a dynamic state model, allowing for continuous evolution and optimization driven by the inherent properties of quantum mechanics. This research contributes to the advancement of quantum simulation and optimization, offering a robust and flexible methodology.

title: On Symbolic Deep Learning: Enhancing Interpretability Through Logical Reasoning
abstract: The increasing deployment of deep learning models in critical applications necessitates a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Current interpretability techniques often provide superficial explanations, failing to reveal the underlying reasoning behind model predictions. This paper proposes a novel approach – Symbolic Deep Learning – that integrates deep learning with symbolic logic to achieve a more robust and transparent understanding of model behavior. We map the output of deep learning models into a symbolic representation, utilizing logical inference algorithms to dissect the model's decision logic. This framework allows us to identify key features driving predictions and uncover potentially unexpected or biased reasoning patterns. The core claim of this work is that by grounding deep learning models in symbolic logic, we can unveil the inherent logic governing their decisions. We present a methodology for translating learned representations into logical forms and demonstrate its potential through a series of illustrative examples. Our approach offers a significant step towards building truly explainable and trustworthy deep learning systems. ---

title: 基于混沌系统的自适应梯度优化算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive gradient optimization algorithm based on the principles of chaos theory. Traditional gradient descent methods often struggle with vanishing gradients, particularly in deep learning scenarios. This algorithm dynamically adjusts the learning rate based on the data's characteristics, mitigating these issues and enhancing the model's generalization ability. We explore the application of chaotic systems, specifically a Lorenz attractor, to generate a unique optimization strategy. The core mechanism involves mapping the learning rate to the attractor's parameters, allowing the algorithm to 'flow' towards optimal solutions more effectively. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in convergence speed and robustness compared to conventional gradient descent methods, particularly in datasets exhibiting complex, non-linear relationships. The algorithm's adaptability and the potential for near-optimal solutions make it a promising approach for a wide range of machine learning applications.

title: Dynamic Trust Mechanism for Asynchronous Multi-Party Computation
abstract: Asynchronous Multi-Party Computation (MPC) offers a powerful paradigm for secure computation without revealing individual inputs. However, a significant challenge in MPC lies in establishing and maintaining trust among the participating parties, particularly in dynamic environments where participants may exhibit varying levels of reliability. This paper proposes a dynamic trust mechanism for MPC, leveraging blockchain technology and machine learning algorithms to address this issue. The core idea is to dynamically adjust trust relationships based on participant behavior and contributions during computations. We introduce a system that continuously assesses participant trustworthiness using a blockchain-based ledger and machine learning models. This approach improves computation efficiency and security by focusing trust on reliable participants, reducing the need for constant verification and minimizing the risk of malicious actors. The proposed mechanism provides a robust solution for MPC in scenarios with evolving participant behavior and uncertainty. ---
